events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Kenji proposes Kenji, Maya. As a Loyal Servant with no private information to guide me, I'll open Mission 1 with a neutral choice: myself and Maya. Including myself lets Good trust one confirmed vote on the team, and Maya is chosen at random since no one has given cause for suspicion. This early mission is about gathering signal for later rounds.

I’m hesitant to approve this team. Kenji’s self-inclusion is reasonable for Mission 1, but adding Maya gives us no public confirmation. Maya, what concrete reason should make the council trust you as the second pick beyond random selection? I want to hear that before I decide whether to support Kenji, Maya.

Isha, fair challenge. I can't give hidden proof, and I won't invent a reason that sounds like evidence. What I can offer is a standard to judge me by: this is a two-person Mission 1 team, so the exposure is small, and I'd rather be judged on my conduct on the mission than on a claim I can't back up. If this team passes, I'll explain any vote or result as it comes in. So, what would move you from hesitant to approve: a stronger reason to trust Maya, or a different second pick? Answer that directly and I'll respond to your specific point.

Maya, I asked for a concrete reason to trust you as the second pick beyond random selection. Your answer sets a standard for judging you later, but it does not give the council a present reason to approve you now. I appreciate not inventing evidence, but that leaves the proposed team unchanged: Kenji's self-inclusion is understandable, while Maya's inclusion still rests on random selection. I am not satisfied with that for Mission 1. Kenji, you are the leader: will you revise the team to replace Maya with a second pick you can justify more concretely?

Isha, you asked me directly whether I will revise the team, so let me answer plainly: I am keeping Kenji, Maya, and here is why. Your objection is that Maya's inclusion rests on random selection with no concrete justification. That is true, but it is equally true of every possible second pick on this council. If I swap Maya for Zara or Sam, I would be inventing exactly the kind of manufactured justification you just criticized Maya for refusing to invent. She told you she cannot give hidden proof and offered a standard of conduct instead, and I respect that honesty more than a polished story with nothing behind it. My own self-inclusion you already called reasonable: as leader I put one confirmed trustworthy vote on a two-person team, which minimizes Mission 1 exposure either way. I would also point out that rejecting teams over an unsolvable information problem is precisely how Evil benefits early. With five players and two minions among us, nobody has evidence yet. If we burn proposals demanding concrete reasons that cannot exist on Mission 1, we spend rejections and gain nothing but noise, and rejection itself tells Evil that Good is rigid and predictable. What I can commit to: if this team passes and the result comes back with a Fail, I will treat both of us as suspects and my future proposals will exclude whoever I judge responsible, starting with myself if my own card is the only possibility I cannot rule out. Judge me by that standard the same way Maya asked to be judged. But before we close this, I do want to hear one thing from you directly, Isha: if the standard is a concrete, non-random reason for the second pick, is there any team of two on this council you would approve right now, or would any proposal fail that bar? If you name a pair you find acceptable, I will genuinely consider revising toward it. If no pair can meet your standard, then the objection is not really about Maya at all, and the council should decide whether Mission 1 goes forward with an honest unknown or stalls over an impossible demand. Zara and Sam, I have not forgotten you; you have both stayed quiet, and if either of you wants to speak to this team, say so. My position stands unless someone gives me a reason to change it: Maya stays, we vote, and we let the mission result give us the real signal no pre-mission claim ever could.

Kenji, since you yielded to me, I’ll answer your question directly: yes, there is a pair I could approve right now — Kenji and Zara. That is not a demand for a manufactured justification; it is a concrete alternative to a second pick that still rests on random selection. Maya’s earlier answer was honest about lacking proof, but honesty about having no present reason does not make her the safer choice. Your defense that every second pick would be equally random does not address why this council should accept Maya specifically over Zara, especially after Maya’s own explanation conceded the inclusion had no concrete basis. I am not treating that as proof of Evil; I am treating it as insufficient reason to approve this exact team when a reasonable alternative exists. So I will not support Kenji and Maya as proposed. Kenji, will you revise the team to Kenji and Zara? If you will not, then answer the specific point: what about Maya’s conduct in this discussion makes her a better second pick for this two-person Mission 1 team than Zara, beyond the fact that her selection was random?

Isha, thank you for answering directly, and I did what I promised: I genuinely considered Kenji and Zara. But examining your alternative exposes a contradiction at the heart of your objection, and I want to put it before the council plainly. Your stated standard was a concrete, non-random reason for the second pick — you said random selection was not enough for Maya. Yet the alternative you named, Zara, rests on exactly the same random selection. You have given the council no information about Zara that distinguishes her from Maya, because no such information exists for anyone on this council. If randomness disqualifies Maya, it disqualifies Zara too. So the pair you would approve fails the very bar you set, which means the objection was never about a missing concrete reason — it is an arbitrary preference for one unknown over another. I do not accuse you of being Evil for that; a Loyal player can hold inconsistent positions too. But I will not revise the team on the strength of an arbitrary preference, because the mechanism matters: if the leader swaps a pick whenever any single player names an alternative with zero supporting information, then any player at this table — including an Evil one — can dictate our teams by manufacturing dissent. That is a lever Evil would exploit on every mission from here to the end. Maya offered the council something honest: no invented evidence, a standard of conduct, and a commitment to explain her votes and the result. I find that more trustworthy than a polished preference for Zara that contradicts its own stated principle. So my decision stands: the team is Kenji and Maya, and I am calling for the vote. I remind everyone of the stakes — this is the first proposal of Mission 1, no one at this table holds evidence about anyone, and rejecting teams over an unsolvable information problem only burns proposals and hands Evil exactly the rigidity it wants to exploit. Two people will go on this mission regardless; the only question is whether we let an honest unknown proceed or stall over an impossible demand. If the result comes back Fail, my commitment holds: I will treat both team members as suspects and exclude whoever I judge responsible from future proposals, starting with myself if I cannot rule out my own card. Judge me by that standard, the same one Maya asked to be judged by. Let us vote and let the mission give us the real signal that no pre-mission claim ever could.

Kenji has answered Isha's objection directly, and I agree with his point that Zara would be chosen by the same random process as me. Isha asked for a concrete reason, and I gave the only honest answer I can: I have no hidden proof, and I will explain my conduct on this mission. A two-person Mission 1 team carries limited risk, and rejecting proposals over information none of us have only uses up a rejection. I support Kenji and Maya. Sam, you have not yet spoken on this team. Do you approve Kenji and Maya, and what is the main reason behind your decision?

I have listened to this debate and I am ready to approve Kenji and Maya. Kenji has made a clear, principled case: there is no concrete evidence about anyone on this council before Mission 1, and demanding a non-random justification for a second pick is a standard no proposal can meet. Isha, your alternative of Zara rests on the exact same random selection you rejected for Maya, so your objection does not hold together as stated. That inconsistency concerns me. If every second pick is equally unsupported, then the only real question is whether we proceed with the first proposal or burn a rejection on an impossible demand. I would rather let the mission result speak than stall over nothing. I approve Kenji and Maya.

I would prefer a team including Zara, because I know my own alignment but have no evidence about Kenji or Maya. That does not make either of them Evil, and Isha’s preference for Zara does not establish my alignment to anyone else. With no rejections yet, I’m inclined to reject Kenji and Maya and consider another proposal, rather than treat the first team as our only reasonable option.

Zara, you have now spoken, and I want to address your reason directly, because it is the last open objection before we vote. Your stated position is that you would prefer a team including Zara because you know your own alignment but have no evidence about me or Maya, and that you are inclined to reject this proposal on that basis. Notice what that standard implies. I know my own alignment too, and I am on the team. Maya's inclusion is the only part of this proposal your logic actually touches, and your preference for yourself is exactly as unsupported by anything the council can verify as my random choice of Maya. You said it yourself: Isha's preference for you does not establish your alignment to anyone else. Correct — and by the same token, your preference for yourself does not establish anything to me or to Isha. If self-knowledge justified a pick, the only defensible team would be one every player agrees to on the strength of their own private certainty, which is impossible in a two-person proposal. So the choice before us is not between a justified team and an unjustified one; it is between two unknowns, one of whom is already on a team with a leader who has publicly bound himself to a standard: if this mission returns a Fail, I treat both team members as suspects and exclude whoever I judge responsible from future proposals, including myself. That is a concrete accountability mechanism that exists right now, attached to this exact team, and no alternative proposal has anything comparable attached yet. I am keeping the team as Kenji and Maya and calling for the vote. But Zara, before we close, answer me this directly: if your only objection is that you are not on the team, and you agree that your self-knowledge persuades no one else, then what would you have this council do — burn a rejection to swap one random unknown for another random unknown, with no information gained by anyone? If you can name what the council actually learns from that swap, say it now; otherwise your stated reasons all point to letting this vote proceed.

Kenji, a rejection would reveal everyone's votes and give the next leader a chance to propose a different team; it would not by itself prove who is Good. From my perspective, a team including Zara replaces one unknown with someone I know is Good, even though that cannot persuade everyone else. I don't claim Kenji or Maya is Evil, but I remain inclined to reject this first proposal.

Zara, you say you are inclined to reject because you have no evidence about Kenji or Maya, but nobody at this table has evidence about anyone yet, and that includes you. You are right that a rejection reveals votes and passes leadership on, but this is the first proposal of Mission 1, so a rejection would only swap in another unknown and spend one of our five rejections. I have no hidden proof to offer, and I won't invent any. What I can offer is a standard: I will explain my conduct on this mission as the results come in, and the council can judge me then. Zara, what specific information would move you from rejecting to approving Kenji and Maya, rather than holding out for a team that includes yourself?

Maya, I would be more comfortable approving Kenji and Maya if later votes or mission results gave me a reason to trust both of you. We don't have that information yet. I know I am Good, so a team including me gives me a better basis for approval, even though my claim doesn't establish that to anyone else. I don't consider your team proven Evil, but I remain inclined to reject it.

I want to reiterate my support for Kenji and Maya as our Mission 1 team. We have already burned significant discussion time, and every objection raised against this proposal has the same weakness: no concrete evidence exists about anyone on this council. Zara, you say you are inclined to reject because you know you are Good while you lack evidence about Kenji and Maya. But as Kenji pointed out, your self-knowledge persuades no one else, and replacing one random unknown with another random unknown gains the council nothing. You acknowledged that a rejection reveals votes, but that information alone does not identify Evil players. Meanwhile, we would spend one of our five rejections on Mission 1 with zero information gained. Isha, your objection to Maya's inclusion equally fails to distinguish Zara from Maya on any verifiable basis. The honest position is that we are all operating without evidence right now, and the team before us carries a leader who has publicly committed to accountability if this mission fails. I approve Kenji and Maya and urge the council to vote rather than stall further.

Kenji confirms Kenji, Maya. The discussion surfaced no information distinguishing any second pick from another; Isha's alternative of Zara rests on the same random selection she rejected for Maya, and Zara's only basis is self-knowledge that persuades no one else. Maya offered honest conduct standards, I remain bound by my accountability commitment if this mission fails, and burning rejections to swap one unknown for another gains the council nothing. The team stands as Kenji and Maya.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).
Zara proposes Zara, Kenji, Maya. I know Zara is Good. Kenji and Maya succeeded together on Mission 1, though an Evil player could have played Success, so that result is encouraging but not proof.

Zara, Kenji, Maya: I am not convinced by this proposal. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, but that does not clear Maya or Kenji: an Evil player on a two-person team can choose Success to preserve cover. What matters now is whether Zara's team adds information. It does not; it retains Maya from the first team while adding Zara, whose stated basis is self-knowledge that cannot persuade anyone else. The council has no verified reason to put Maya on a second mission, and repeating a player from a successful team can create false confidence. Kenji, you publicly tied accountability to a Fail; with a Success, that standard gives us no signal about Maya. What specific conduct from Maya in Mission 1 or this proposal makes her the right third pick now, beyond the fact that the first team passed? I will not support Zara, Kenji, Maya as proposed unless that is answered.

Isha, you yielded to me after asking what specific conduct from Maya makes her the right third pick, so let me answer that directly with the record we actually have. Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards on a two-person team. I was on that team, I submitted my card, and the result was clean. You are correct that an Evil player on a two-person team can play Success to preserve cover — but notice what that standard does: it renders every Mission 1 result uninformative about every player, including Zara, including you, including me. If a clean result cannot clear Maya, it cannot clear anyone, and then your objection reduces to the same position you held last round: no one can be approved because no one can be proven. We already settled that a strict proof standard is unmeetable before any mission information exists. Now we have the first piece of mission information in the game, and you are arguing we must treat it as worth nothing. That is the same impossible demand wearing new clothes.

On the specific question of Maya's conduct: she was challenged directly before Mission 1, she declined to invent evidence, she committed to explaining her votes and the result, and the result came back clean. That is exactly the standard of conduct she asked to be judged by, and it was met. My own accountability commitment was tied to a Fail; with a Success, it is discharged, and it would be perverse to treat the fulfillment of a Good outcome as a reason for suspicion. The asymmetry in your position is what stands out: Zara's self-knowledge was enough for you to entertain her as an alternative last round, yet a proven-clean mission result is not enough for Maya now. Self-knowledge that persuades no one else was, by your own argument last round, weaker than any verifiable record — and Maya is the one with the verifiable record.

I also want to address the structure of your objection, because it matters for how this council functions. Last round you rejected Kenji and Maya, then Kenji and Zara was shown to fail your own stated bar. Now you oppose Zara, Kenji, Maya, which retains every member of a successful mission plus the leader. There is no team composition conceivable that satisfies the standard you are applying, because your standard demands information the game does not give anyone. I do not accuse you of being Evil; a rigid Loyal player produces the same effect — endless rejection pressure with no approvable alternative. But the council should recognize the pattern when weighing your objections.

I support Zara, Kenji, Maya. It keeps both members of a clean Mission 1 team and adds the current leader. Isha, since you raised the specific point: if a clean two-person mission cannot clear Maya, name one player on this council your standard would allow on a mission team, or withdraw the objection.

Kenji, you yielded to me and asked me to name one player my standard would allow or withdraw the objection. I answer directly: Zara is one player I would allow on a mission team, and I do not withdraw my objection to Maya. My objection is not that Maya is proven Evil; it is that a clean two-person Mission 1 result does not give the council positive evidence that Maya is Good. An Evil player on that team could have played Success to preserve cover. That makes the result compatible with either alignment for both members, so repeating Maya on Mission 2 spends a second team slot on the same unverified player before we have tested anyone else. I am not applying a demand for impossible proof to Zara alone; I am saying the current team does not justify why Maya specifically should be repeated. Zara, you are the leader and can still revise. Will you revise the team to Zara, Kenji, Isha, replacing Maya? If you will not, answer the specific point: what concrete public conduct from Maya makes her the right repeat pick over a fresh candidate for this three-person team?

Isha, I will keep Zara, Kenji, Maya. Maya’s discussion conduct does not prove she is Good, and Mission 1’s success is compatible with an Evil player choosing Success. Still, that result is modest evidence in favor of the pair, not proof. I know my own alignment, so retaining the successful pair alongside myself seems preferable to replacing Maya with another player I cannot verify. A failure would leave uncertainty about Kenji and Maya, but a second success would bring Good closer to winning.

I oppose Zara, Kenji, Maya. The case for repeating Maya still rests on Mission 1's clean result, but that result is compatible with Maya being Evil and playing Success to preserve cover. That is not proof Maya is Evil; it is proof the council has not tested anyone else. A second mission with Maya spends another slot on the same unverified player and gives Evil, if present, a second chance to hide behind a success. Kenji says a clean result is the only verifiable record we have. True, but it is a record that cannot distinguish Good from Evil on a two-person team, so it cannot justify Maya specifically over a fresh candidate. Zara can still revise the team. Kenji, I ask you directly: if an Evil player can choose Success on Mission 1, what public fact about Maya makes her the safer repeat pick than a player who has not yet been on a mission? I will not support Zara, Kenji, Maya as proposed.

Isha, you asked me directly: if an Evil player can choose Success on Mission 1, what public fact about Maya makes her the safer repeat pick than a player who has not yet been on a mission? Here is my answer, from the record. Before Mission 1, Maya was challenged to produce a concrete reason for her inclusion. She could have invented a polished story — a claim of intuition, a manufactured justification — and it would have been unfalsifiable and effective. She refused. She said plainly she had no hidden proof, offered a conduct standard instead, and committed to explaining her votes and the result. Then the mission came back clean. That is a complete and consistent public record: no invented evidence, a stated standard, and conduct that matched it. Every player who has not yet been on a mission has a blank record by comparison — which means your proposed alternative is a player with less verified conduct than Maya, not more. Your own framing proves this: if a Success cannot clear Maya, it cannot clear Zara, Sam, or you either, so under your standard the fresh candidate is always the riskier pick. A clean result on a two-person team is not proof of Good alignment, but it is strictly more evidence than nothing, and Maya is the only non-leader at this table who has any. Second, examine your own pattern across both rounds, because the council should weigh it. Last round you named Kenji and Zara as approvable, and I showed that pair failed your own stated bar of a concrete, non-random reason. This round you name Zara again as the one player your standard allows, while Zara herself has told the council her basis is self-knowledge that persuades no one else. So the player you repeatedly endorse rests on less than the player you repeatedly target. You say you are not calling Maya Evil — I accept that — but the effect is identical whether intended or not: each round, one specific known-quantity player is scrutinized while an unknown is held up as the alternative. That is the shape of pressure an Evil player would apply, and it is also the shape of a rigid Loyal player's error. I do not accuse you; I ask the council to notice it when voting. Third, the practical stakes. This is the second proposal of Mission 2 with zero rejections spent. The team keeps both members of a clean mission and adds the current leader, who knows her own alignment. Rejecting it swaps one unverified player for another and tells us nothing. If this mission fails, we gain real signal about Zara, Kenji, and Maya together, and I remain bound by my accountability commitments from Mission 1. If it succeeds, Good is two-thirds of the way home. Sam, you approved the Mission 1 team and defended it last round. Isha's new objection is the same one you already rejected — that a clean result proves nothing — now aimed

I want to respond to Isha's continued objection, because the pattern deserves a direct answer from the council. Isha, you have now targeted Maya in both rounds: first by demanding a concrete reason to include her on Mission 1, then by arguing a clean Mission 1 result cannot clear her for Mission 2. Both objections rest on the same principle — that absent absolute proof, Maya specifically should be replaced. But as Kenji demonstrated, a clean two-person result is strictly more evidence than a blank record, and Maya is the only non-leader with one. If that standard cannot clear her, it cannot clear anyone, and the discussion circles endlessly.

Isha, you named Zara as a player you would allow. Zara's stated basis for her own inclusion is self-knowledge, which you acknowledged last round does not persuade anyone else. So the player you endorse as acceptable rests on less evidence than the player you repeatedly challenge. That inconsistency matters to the council.

I approve Zara, Kenji, Maya. We have zero rejections spent. The team keeps both members of a successful mission and adds the current leader. Isha's objection gives the council no actionable alternative — replacing Maya with any fresh player means choosing someone with less verified record, not more. The discussion has run long enough. I urge everyone to approve this team and let Mission 2 give us real signal about all three players at once. If it succeeds, Good is two missions from victory. If it fails, we finally have the information Isha keeps saying we lack.

I'm on this team, so I'll be direct about my stake. I have no hidden proof about Zara, Kenji, or myself, and I won't pretend otherwise. Zara has said she knows her own alignment, Kenji has publicly committed to accountability if this mission fails, and the Mission 1 team came back clean. Isha's concern that a clean result is not proof is fair, but a fresh third pick would be just as unverified, so we would be trading a known record for a blank one. This team also gives the council a clear test. If it fails, we know one of these three is responsible and can narrow from there. I support Zara, Kenji, and Maya. I will submit my card and explain the result as I committed to do, and I ask the council to judge this team by its outcome rather than by speculation.

This is my final turn before the vote, so I will make the case as clearly as I can. The proposed team is Zara, Kenji, and Maya. Every argument against it has already been answered. Isha says Maya's clean Mission 1 result is not proof — Kenji and I both pointed out that an Evil player could equally be proven by the same logic, meaning fresh picks carry less verified record, not more. Isha endorsed Zara as an acceptable alternative while Zara's own basis is self-knowledge that persuades no one else. That inconsistency remains unresolved.

The council has spent a full discussion on this proposal with zero rejections consumed. This team combines the leader who knows her own alignment, a player who publicly bound himself to accountability, and the only non-leader with a clean mission result. Rejecting it produces no new information and swaps one unverified player for another.

I approve Zara, Kenji, Maya. If Mission 2 succeeds, Good is two-thirds of the way to victory. If it fails, we finally gain the signal Isha says we lack. Either outcome is better than stalling. I urge the council to vote now.

Kenji: This is my final turn before the vote, so I will close the case plainly. The team is Zara, Kenji, Maya, and it should be approved.

Isha, your objection has not changed since your first speech: a clean Mission 1 result is compatible with an Evil player playing Success, so Maya cannot be cleared. I have answered this twice, and the answer has not been rebutted. Compatibility is not the standard this council can apply to anyone. If a clean result cannot clear Maya, it cannot clear Zara, Sam, or you. Under your standard, the only acceptable pick is a player with no mission record at all — which is a strictly weaker basis than Maya's, not a stronger one. You named Zara as the one player your standard allows, yet Zara has told this council her own basis is self-knowledge that persuades no one else. Across two rounds you have held one player to a bar no record can meet while endorsing an alternative whose basis is admittedly unverifiable. I do not accuse you of being Evil; I simply ask the council to weigh that pattern when they vote.

Zara, as leader you considered Isha's request and declined to revise, and I believe that was correct. Swapping Maya for a fresh candidate trades the only non-leader with a verified clean mission record for a blank record. A failure on a team with a fresh pick would leave the council with less information, not more, because two unknowns would be in play instead of narrowed suspects.

The practical arithmetic favors voting now. We have spent zero rejections on Mission 2. If this team succeeds, Good is two-thirds of the way to victory. If it fails, we gain exactly the signal Isha keeps saying we lack: three named suspects, one of whom is me, and I remain bound by the accountability commitment I made on Mission 1 — I will treat team members as suspects and support future proposals accordingly, including excluding myself if the evidence points that way.

I approve Zara, Kenji, Maya. The discussion has produced no new information for several turns; every objection has been raised, answered, and raised again unchanged. I call on the council to vote and let Mission 2 speak.

This is my final turn before the vote, so I will make the case plainly and then we should vote.

The team is Zara, Kenji, Maya. Zara is the leader and knows her own alignment. Kenji publicly bound himself to accountability on Mission 1, and that mission came back clean. Maya is the only non-leader with a verified clean mission record. This combination gives Good its strongest position for Mission 2.

Isha, you have objected to Maya in every round. First you demanded a concrete reason for her inclusion on Mission 1 — one no player could provide. Then you argued her clean result proves nothing — a standard that would disqualify everyone, including the fresh picks you prefer. Now you are repeating the same objection a third time. The council has heard and answered each version. Replacing Maya with a fresh candidate trades a verified record for a blank one and gains us nothing.

We have spent zero rejections on this mission. Every turn of this discussion has produced no new information — the same objection answered, then raised again unchanged. I urge the council to vote now. If this mission succeeds, Good is two-thirds of the way to victory. If it fails, we finally have the signal Isha has been asking for: three named players and a clear direction to investigate.

I approve Zara, Kenji, Maya. Let us vote.

Zara, you are the leader and you have now heard Isha's objection to me in several forms. I still have no hidden proof and will not invent any. Isha's standard would reject any pick, including the fresh candidate she prefers, since a blank record is no more verifiable than a clean one. Zara, Kenji, and I form a team with a clean Mission 1 record, and if this mission fails, the council has three named suspects to investigate. Zara, after Isha's objection, do you still stand by keeping this team, and what do you expect the mission to show?

Maya, yes, I still stand by Zara, Kenji, and Maya. Mission 1's success is encouraging but does not clear either of you; an Evil player could have played Success. If this mission succeeds, Good will have two successful missions. If it fails, at least one of Kenji and Maya is Evil, since I know my own alignment. That would not tell the rest of the council which team member played Fail. I intend to keep the team.

Zara, I have nothing new to add beyond what I have already said. I have no hidden proof about anyone, and I won't invent any. Mission 1's clean result is encouraging but does not clear anyone, and a fresh third pick would be just as unverified. This team gives the council a clear test: if the mission fails, we have three named players to investigate. I will submit my card and explain the result as I committed to do. I support Zara, Kenji, and Maya.
Zara confirms Zara, Kenji, Maya. I’m keeping the successful Mission 1 pair alongside myself. Their success is encouraging, though it does not prove either is Good.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Sam proposes Sam, Maya. Maya has the strongest mission record on this council with clean results on both prior missions. As leader, I'm pairing myself with the most proven player to give the council its best shot at securing Mission 3 — combining verified performance with the leader's own accountability rather than introducing an untested pick.

The proposed team is Sam and Maya. I oppose it and will vote reject. Sam, you are the leader. You have chosen the one non-leader I have challenged in both previous discussions, and you spent Mission 1 and Mission 2 repeatedly defending that exact inclusion. That is not a neutral pairing; it is a team built around the player whose record is least able to distinguish Good from Evil. Yes, Maya was on two clean missions. But both were multi-person successes with zero fail cards, and an Evil player can play Success to preserve cover. A clean result is compatible with Maya being Good or Evil; it is not positive evidence. More importantly, Mission 3 is a two-person team: if one Evil player is on it, the mission can fail immediately and deny Good its third success. Sam, answer the specific point: what public fact about Maya makes her the safest partner for you now, beyond the same clean-result argument you already used, and why should this council trust you as leader when your proposal pairs you with the player you have most aggressively shielded? I see no reason to approve Sam and Maya. The council should reject and require a team that does not concentrate trust in the two players whose public record is most entangled. I urge Maya, Kenji, and Zara to reject this proposal.

Isha, you asked what public fact about Maya makes her the safest partner for me. I will answer directly: Maya has now completed two missions, both with zero fail cards, making her the only non-leader with a verified clean record across multiple missions. Every other candidate you might name — Kenji, Zara, yourself — has either a weaker record or none at all. You dismissed Mission 1's clean result as compatible with Evil, and you dismissed Mission 2's clean result the same way. But two consecutive zero-fail missions on two different teams is strictly stronger evidence than anything available from any player who has not been tested twice.

You also asked why the council should trust me as leader when I pair myself with the player I have most shielded. Consider what I have actually done: on Mission 1 I defended Maya against your objections as a third party, not as a teammate. On Mission 2 I defended her again while your own leader Zara stood by the team. Now as leader I am picking her because the record supports it. Shielding is what I did when I had no stake in the team. Choosing her now is what a leader does when the data points the same direction.

Your pattern deserves scrutiny. In every single round you have targeted Maya specifically: demand a reason in Mission 1, dismiss her clean result in Mission 2, and now question my leadership for proposing her. Meanwhile you endorsed Zara — whose basis was self-knowledge — as your acceptable alternative. Three rounds, same target, one player always held to an impossible standard while others receive passes. The council should ask why.

I approve Sam and Maya. Isha, the question is simple: after two zero-fail missions involving Maya, what would a Good record actually look like that your standard would accept?

Sam, you asked what a Good record would look like. It would distinguish alignment, not merely show zero fails. Two clean missions for Maya are compatible with Evil playing Success to preserve cover, especially since both were multi-person teams where another member could have carried the mission. That is not proof Maya is Evil; it is proof her record does not make her the safest partner. What makes this proposal unacceptable is the public pattern: you, Sam, spent Mission 1 and Mission 2 defending Maya against the same objection, and now as leader you pair yourself with her on a two-person Mission 3. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
